name: The Rust Circuit
description:
Euclid was a manufacturing suburb. The factories that lined East 185th Street and the lakefront produced machine tools, auto parts, and industrial equipment for a century before the work went elsewhere — first to the American South, then overseas, then to automation, then to the corridor's corporate manufacturing zones where human labor was an afterthought rather than a workforce. By 2140, Euclid's factory district was a graveyard of corrugated steel and broken windows. By 2160, it was something else entirely.

The Rust Circuit is the eastern corridor's informal technology and repair economy — a sprawling district of repurposed factories where independent engineers, mechanics, augment technicians, and fabricators operate outside corporate licensing frameworks. The name is self-aware: this is the rust belt's final form, where the industrial infrastructure built for 20th-century manufacturing has been adapted for 22nd-century work by people who couldn't afford to start from scratch. The factories that once produced auto parts now produce augment components. The machine shops that serviced industrial equipment now service neural interfaces. The skills transferred across a century because the underlying logic is the same — precision fabrication, mechanical intuition, the ability to make something work when the manual says it shouldn't.

The Circuit East (as it's called to distinguish it from GLMZ's original Circuit near the Meridian Core) functions as the Cleveland sprawl's repair shop. If your augments need maintenance and you can't afford Tessera's service contracts, you come to the Rust Circuit. If your equipment needs modification and you don't want a corponation knowing what you're modifying, you come to the Rust Circuit. If you need something built that doesn't exist in any corporate catalog, you come to the Rust Circuit and describe it to someone who will nod, quote you a price in scrip or favors, and have it ready in a week. The quality is inconsistent — this is unlicensed work, and the range runs from genuinely brilliant to dangerously incompetent — but the availability is unmatched. The Rust Circuit never closes, never asks for identification, and never files paperwork.

sights: Repurposed factory buildings with hand-painted signage advertising augment repair, fabrication, and services that don't have official names
Sparks from welding and fabrication visible through open factory doors at all hours — the Rust Circuit operates on a 24-hour cycle
Salvage yards organized with obsessive precision — components sorted by type, era, and compatibility in systems that only the yard operators understand
Lake Erie visible from the northern factories, its shoreline littered with industrial debris that has been scavenged so thoroughly it's become a kind of art
Operators and clients moving through the streets with the particular body language of people conducting business they'd prefer not to explain
sounds: Machine noise — lathes, presses, welders, and fabrication equipment running in every factory, creating a metallic symphony that changes block to block
Augment calibration tones — high-frequency whines that indicate someone's neural interface is being adjusted, tested, or rebuilt
Haggling — prices negotiated in a mix of Standard, Shelf Cant, and the particular technical shorthand that Rust Circuit workers have developed
The screech of metal being cut — a sound that never fully stops and that residents claim to hear in their sleep
Testing — the occasional pop, bang, or alarming silence that indicates someone is testing something they've built and discovering whether it works
smells: Machine oil and hot metal — the baseline scent of every block in the Rust Circuit
Soldering flux — the sharp, resinous smell of circuit board work, omnipresent near the augment repair shops
Lake Erie's industrial shoreline — a blend of water, rust, and chemical residue that residents call 'the perfume'
atmosphere.feel: The Rust Circuit feels like competence without credentials. Everyone here can do something — build something, fix something, modify something — and the social currency is demonstrated skill rather than corporate certification. It is chaotic, loud, and occasionally dangerous in the way that any place filled with improvised technology and unlicensed expertise is dangerous. But it works. The things built here work. The things repaired here work. And in a corridor where 'working' increasingly means 'under corporate control,' that independence is worth the risk.

demographics: Approximately 30,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1-2. A core population of multi-generational Euclid families whose industrial skills translated across the century. Significant influx of technical workers priced out of the Meridian Core's Circuit. Growing population of augmented individuals who have been cut off from corporate maintenance contracts and depend on the Rust Circuit for survival.
economy: Unlicensed repair, fabrication, and manufacturing. The Rust Circuit's annual economic output is estimated at Φ2.8 billion — entirely informal, entirely untaxed, and entirely essential to the Cleveland sprawl's lower-tier population. Augment maintenance is the highest-volume service. Custom fabrication is the highest-value. Salvage processing generates steady baseline revenue.
power_structure: No corporate sovereignty. Tollgate maintains minimum infrastructure. Governance operates through the Shop Council — a representative body of the district's largest fabrication operations, which sets quality standards, mediates disputes, and coordinates collective response to external threats. The Council's enforcement mechanism is reputation: a shop that the Council blacklists loses access to the supply networks and referral systems that make the Rust Circuit function.
dangers: Quality variance — unlicensed augment work ranges from excellent to lethal, and the customer bears the risk
No legal protections — transactions in the Rust Circuit have no corporate backing, no warranty, and no recourse
Tessera enforcement — periodic raids targeting unlicensed augment maintenance operations, which Tessera frames as 'consumer protection' and everyone else frames as monopoly enforcement
Industrial hazards — the repurposed factories were never designed for their current uses, and safety standards are self-imposed
Data vulnerability — some augment repair work requires deep interface access that a dishonest technician can exploit
opportunities: Access to repair and fabrication services unavailable through corporate channels — essential for operators, runners, and anyone whose equipment is non-standard
The Shop Council's reputation network is a valuable social infrastructure — being known in the Rust Circuit means being known across the Cleveland sprawl's excluded economy
Technical talent — the Rust Circuit's independent engineers and fabricators are among the most skilled practical technologists in the corridor
Supply chain access — the salvage yards connect to scavenging networks that reach across the eastern corridor, providing materials and components at gray-market prices
story_hooks: A Rust Circuit fabricator has built an augment component that outperforms Tessera's commercial equivalent by a factor of three — and Tessera wants to know how, preferably before anyone else finds out
The Shop Council has received an ultimatum from Tollgate: submit to infrastructure licensing and taxation, or face service disconnection. The deadline is sixty days.
An augment repair technician has discovered identical tracking devices embedded in three different clients' neural interfaces — devices that don't match any known corponation's surveillance hardware
frequented_by: Operators, runners, and anyone whose equipment needs off-book maintenance
Augmented individuals cut off from corporate service contracts
Fixers sourcing custom equipment and modifications
Tessera enforcement agents, unwelcome and easily identified

notable_locations.name: The 185th Street Fabrication Row
notable_locations.description: The densest concentration of independent machine shops and fabrication operations in the eastern corridor — if it can be built, someone on 185th can build it

notable_locations.name: The Lakeshore Yards
notable_locations.description: Salvage processing operations along Euclid's industrial shoreline — the raw material supply chain for the entire Rust Circuit

notable_locations.name: The Shop Council Hall
notable_locations.description: A converted factory floor where the district's governing body meets — dispute resolution, standard-setting, and the closest thing the Rust Circuit has to a courthouse
